utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to the information that I have, the village of Zegra was a rather highly developed village. There was a factory there, Jugoterm, where Serbs and Albanians worked, and also the agricultural combine Mladost, and there were paved roads, and there was electricity, running water, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Partly true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Zegra was never bombed or shelled by the army and police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not accurate because the police and the army, the Serb police and army, have burned down the village of Zheger. But what the accused said is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about later? Was it NATO first and then the KLA that shelled and bombed the village of Budrike, six kilometres away from Zegra on the road to Gnjilane? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the village of Budrike, there was no KLA forces there. The village is inhabited entirely by the Serbs, and the bombing, the NATO bombing, was carried out in those areas where the Serb forces were deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that is correct.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it's -- it's not true. It's partly not true because there was no KLA shelling of the Budrike village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. At the medical centre in Gnjilane, there were 370 Albanian employees; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the medical centre of the hospital of Gjilan, before the NATO bombing, there were also Albanian doctors. But after the beginning of the NATO bombing, the Albanian personnel left the hospital, and that was under the orders of the Serb officials who were in charge there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that there were 370 Albanian employees at the medical centre in Gnjilane?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the situation before the war. Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they left on orders given by the KLA; right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just give a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I am saying no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Also, the technical school in Gnjilane was attended by 405 Albanians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which school are we talking about? The technical school? The schools in general were segregated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said it quite clearly: the technical school.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the technical school is concerned, there were no Albanians there, because there was segregation in the school. The Serbs were studying separately from the Albanians since 1990, when the Kosovo autonomy -- when Kosovo was stripped of its autonomy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the difference between the education of the Serbs and the education of the Albanians, except for language?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some curricula and programmes which the Albanians did not accept. They were from the Serbo-Slav Federation. But we had our own national programmes, and hence the differences in history, language, music, but also in the exact sciences. But they are of a different nature, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the difference as far as natural sciences were concerned?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference can be explained by the competent people who have drafted those programmes. I do not know the difference between the Albanian and the Serbian programmes, but we have been working on the basis of the Albanian programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For Albanian children, schooling was in the Albanian language, and for Serb children, in the Serb language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but the school programmes were different. Lessons for the Albanian students was taking place in the houses-turned-schools, whereas the Serbs were studying in the school premises, and the same thing took place from the elementary schools to the university level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you whether schooling was in Albanian for Albanians and in Serbian for the Serbs. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that was the case, but I also explained that the teaching was segregated, and that was being organised on the basis of different programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Teaching was separate in terms of language; yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's dealt twice with that. He said that schooling was in the different languages. I think we could move on now, Mr. Milosevic, from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You did not answer my question whether it is correct that 405 Albanians attended the technical school. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, if you don't know, just say so.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards this one, I don't know. And the school that the accused is talking about did not exist. This is something that maybe the accused is imagining.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The economic school -- the economic school, the school of economics, was attended by 952 Albanians, and that was in 1999, at that. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The economic school -- I said earlier that all the schools, the economic included, were segregated, and the Albanians were conducting teaching on the basis of the special Albanian programmes, which were different from those of the Serb system, educational system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you're a teacher, you know full well that when a teacher enters a classroom, he teaches whatever he wishes to teach. I'm not asking about the programme, the curriculum; I'm just asking you whether it is true that 952 Albanians were attending the economic school in 1999. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already talked about these elements. I've nothing else to say on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You talked about the technical school. You did not talk about the economic school.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked about the technical school, and I said that the technical school, the economic school, and all the schools in the Gjilan area, they were segregated because the system operated on a different basis from that of the Serb educational system, and it operated on the basis of programmes that were designed, that were drafted by the institutions of the Kosova republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is not being contested whether Serbs studied in Serbian and Albanians in Albanian. Of course that was separate. I'm saying, did they go to school? You are not answering that question. And I claim that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, he has answered that. He said that they did. Now, let's move on to another topic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Zegra itself there were 758 students, Albanians, 79 Serb students, pupils; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Zegra, in your village, there were 758 pupils, 79 Serb pupils. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many Albanian pupils were there at the school in Zegra?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of the Albanian -- the number of students in the Zheger school was about 900, and as for the Serb students, they were a small number, about 30, 20 to 30, because the Serbian population in the village was very small. There were a few kids there. The number of Serb students between the first and the fourth grade of the elementary schools was small, and they took part in combined classes. So there were students who were -- teachers who were conducting teaching of students in two levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Seven hundred fifty-eight students plus 79 students gives a total of about 900, as you have just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they went to school, not to private houses.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The teaching in the elementary school of Zheger was taking place in the school premises, but the teaching was taking place on the basis of programmes that were drafted by Kosova, by the Republic of Kosova, and they were national programmes and not programmes designed by the Ministry of Education in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the programme. I'm asking you -- I'm saying that they went to a state school, not to a private house.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that a state school is the one which is protected by the state and when it's been used by Albanian students, but they were using quite different programmes, different from those of the state, and this is not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. They went to a state school; yes or no.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his answer and qualifications.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember your fellow citizens, Blerim Hyseni, the police took two pistols away from him?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember when and if that happened. I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember Jahija Bislimi? He was employed at the Municipal Assembly of Gnjilane and a rifle was taken away from him.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand who we are talking about. Jamija, Jahija, it does not exist in Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is not Jahija, it is Jahi Bislimi. He was an employee of the Municipal Assembly of Gnjilane and a rifle was taken away from him.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know a person with this name and surname in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember Esad Bidaku? An automatic rifle was also taken away from him. He's also from your village.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This name too, Esad Bidaku, does not exist in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about Mehdi Musliu? Does a person by that name exist in your village?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mehdi Musliu? With this particular name -- a person with this particular name that you mentioned does not exist. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What about -- I mean, since you don't know any one of these villagers of yours, what about your brother, Shaban Shabani? Did you have a brother called Shaban Shabani?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. He died in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that your brother, your older brother, Shaban Shabani, before the bombing, as a member of the KLA, went to Albania and got killed as he was crossing the border from Albania, as he was returning with his group; he was killed in a clash with the army of Yugoslavia during the month of April?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true. About this case, I want to give my explanation to the Court and show what the reality is. Your Honours, my brother, Shaban Shabani, was a retired man. He retired as an invalid because he was suffering from heart disease. But when in Albania there was democratic change, he went there to recover from his illness. After he went to Albania, he died from a heart attack in Dures. Together with my brothers Refik Shabani and Ibrahim Shabani, we went to collect the corpse, the body of my brother, in Albania, and we did not have permission from the Serb Ministry of Interior. That's why we got across the border. And I want to tell you that what the accused is saying is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would you repeat again when it was your brother died.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When the war broke out, that is to say, on the eve of the 24th of March, you were principal of secondary education in Zegra; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not the principal of the secondary school in Zheger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say secondary school; I said secondary education, this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. secondary education that you organised, and you appointed people as to who would teach what, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't the person who appointed teachers either. That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you said that it is not correct that your brother was killed as he was crossing the border, do you know about Agim Ramadani, a former officer of the JNA who was killed as he was crossing the border at Kosare, and he was buried in Zegra a few days later? You spoke on the anniversary of his death, and this was attended by Hasim Thaci, because he was one of the terrorists of his. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Agim Ramadani is concerned, it's true that he took part in the battle of Koshare, and he was the commander of one of the units in Koshare, and he was killed on the 11th of April, 1993 in Koshare. As far as Hasim Thaci being in Gjilan on the occasion of the solemn meeting organised, this is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you speak at this anniversary of Agim Ramadani's death?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not speak. There were others who did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm just asking you. You just say yes or no. Let us save time. Before the NATO aggression in the second half of 1998 and in 1999, you made lists of all Albanians from Zegra who were of age so that they could join the KLA; yes or no.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't do such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the mobilisation that was proclaimed by the KLA in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the mobilisation, I have heard through the radio and television nothing more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware that in Zegra, in the village of Lashtica, in the immediate vicinity, the police seized 150 automatic rifles, 80 short guns, Scorpions, pistols, Hecklers, 7 sniper rifles, and that there were 7 sniper positions in the territory of Zegra? Do you know about all of this?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are not true. The police, before the war, beginning from 1999 onwards - sorry - beginning from 1990 onwards, it has always taken retaliation actions in our village and has always accused our inhabitants of possessing illegal arms. They have maltreated people. There are two people who have been mistreated, and both of them died. I might give you the names. Mehmet Hajrullah and Salih Isufetahu, who died as a result of that. Mehmet Hajrullah, after he was released from the detention, he died in his own home. The other one, Salih Isufetahu, he died after a month after he was released and tortured by the Serb police. There are other people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to go, at this moment, into detail. If you answer the question shortly, Mr. Shabani, we'll get on more quickly. The Prosecution will have a chance to ask you some more questions at the end if there is anything which needs clarifying. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So would you please give me a yes or no answer to the following question: Do you know about the fact that these 150 automatic rifles were taken away, and the others, the 80, the seven snipers and all the other things that I enumerated, the 80 short guns, et cetera? Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said it wasn't true. He said it wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that after the 10th of June, when the French withdrew from your area and the Americans took over in the territory, that 150 terrorists of the KLA arrived from Macedonia via the village of Stantici on the Macedonian border in the middle of Zegra village and this same man, Esad Bidaku, toured the KLA and you attended this ceremony? Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are getting interference from the Albanian interpretation channel. We apologise.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true. I'm not aware of these things. When I arrived from Macedonia, it was on the 26th of June. Therefore, I am not aware of all these things that you are enumerating here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you here a yes or no answer, please. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said no, I am not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What about the police station in Zegra? Sadih Sofi worked there, a policeman, an Albanian. He lived in a state-owned apartment with his wife and three children. The KLA stormed his apartment, beat him up, raped his wife and beat up his children. Do you know of that event?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that the personality Sofi, as you say, he was beaten by the police. He was in the service of the Serbian police, but after that, the police were no longer there. I know that he went to Gjilan, but I don't know anything about his whereabouts after that, after he was -- if he was beaten by the KLA or other things. I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to something you do know about. You said that the forces of the Yugoslav army arrived in Zegra ten days before the bombing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. About ten, 20 days ago they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Ten or 20 days. It doesn't matter. Yesterday you said ten. If you're saying 20 now, I don't mind. It makes no difference to me. You said that they dug trenches, and then you explained that they prepared to defend themselves against NATO. As you said that they arrived and dug trenches and prepared to defend themselves from NATO - and those were your words yesterday, you spoke those words - did you deduce from that that there was a possible front line being set up there?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a matter for the Serbs to take positions the way they thought they deemed better for them along the valley of Reke in Zheger village. They took positions there. That was their own decision, to defend themselves from NATO strikes, from land or airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you conclude that this was a possible front line, then?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that was a front line because they wanted to fight with the KLA because there was no KLA there, but I think that was their decision, to prepare themselves for an eventual outside intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about that intervention. So they were there to defend themselves from this outside intervention, and then I assumed that it was a sort of front line. Is that right? Possible front line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered that as best he can, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you want to get away from that front line and take refuge from it?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had our own homes. I don't think that it was a good thing to have the front line in the village. The Albanian population of Zheger village were displaced and killed and injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back to that. You spoke about that yesterday. You said that when the bombing started, as you said, the Serb forces became even more furious and wild. How did you come to that conclusion that they became more furious and wild? Did they froth at the mouth or what manner of -- what way did this wildness manifest itself?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The savagery was manifested in the way they treated the people, which is they started to mistreat, to beat the people, to fire at the roofs of the houses of Albanians, to insult the Albanians who passed by in the streets or even to -- to do -- to commit many other such acts against the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday, throughout your testimony, you did not demonstrate to us that anything happened to anybody. You said you yourself went to Macedonia, and we'll get to that in just a moment. So how did they manifest this behaviour of theirs? How did they go wild?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's just said that. He said in the way they treated the people, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the event that took place on the 29th of March and the arrival of some sort of paramilitary, and then you went on to say that you had heard about that. The Prosecutor asked you what their uniform looked like, and you said you didn't see anything. You said that your house was a long way off. So, in fact, you yourself did not see them. You just heard about them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there were other eyewitnesses whose houses were located closer to the school and to those places where these forces took position, these paramilitaries that I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what, according to you, is "paramilitary," Mr. Shabani? Could you explain to us? What do you mean by "paramilitary"?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, a paramilitary is an armed man who commits criminal deeds on the basis of certain well-programmed objectives by certain people with the sole purpose of defending the army or the police to make believe that they are not involved in the murder of the citizens. This was a common phenomenon in the Serbian army. This happened in the Bosnia war and all the time. The paramilitaries were used to help displace the population from their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now moving from the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How can you differentiate between the paramilitary and the army?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can differentiate between them in the way they were dressed. The paramilitary were -- used some handkerchiefs, and they took part in murders and were more savage and prepared to commit murders at any moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as the readiness to commit murders, you said yourself here that the Serb population was preparing to liquidate the Albanians, and you were talking about the time at the beginning of the aggression. Were you yourself liquidated? Did they liquidate you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did you yourself suffer any beating or anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already told you that I myself did not, but they fired at me when I was going away, when I was leaving, along with the other civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they didn't hit you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fortunately, no. Fortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they hit anybody?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They hit and injured other people who were in the convoy. We have two cases, a male and a female, who were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in the convoy, two people were wounded out of all that shooting that went on. Now, you said that they were preparing to liquidate you. What, in your opinion, prevented them from liquidating you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what aims they had at that moment, but I know that they wanted to kill some and to deport the others. That was the main goal of theirs. And this came true in the case of our village, I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. How do you know that they were preparing to liquidate you and then they didn't liquidate you? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew -- we heard this, that some Serbian citizens said that they had prepared the lists of Albanians who had some authority in the village of Zheger whom they wanted to liquidate, to do away with, and the list was there in place, and it waited to be realised, which in fact it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means you were liquidated, were you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to answer that question. It's a comment. Yes. Now, anything else, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I have something else, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you became afraid, that you were frightened of that liquidation, and that you went out, that there were 1.200 people, and that it was raining; is that right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. When murders, injuries, were committed, we were scared and panicky and left our homes and took to the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as it was raining, you went back inside, into the house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the next day, in the morning, because we spent the night outside under the rain, all together, women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the next day you returned, you went back, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My house happened to be situated very close to Kushlevica Hill, but other citizens whose houses were situated in the hinterland of the village, they stayed at our own homes, fearing that the situation Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. might be repeated, so they stayed with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you fled after the killing and wounding. Who was killed and wounded that you had to flee [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that the brother of Shyqeri Tahiri was killed. Their aim was to liquidate Tahir Tahiri, his brother, the chairman of the LDK. Then Nexharije Tahiri was also injured. She is a relative of Shyqeri Tahiri and Tahir Tahiri. So their families and other families heard of this, of what was happening. Other people who were beaten and traumatised as a result of the mistreatment, they all were scared and they all took to the hills of Kushlevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who killed Tahir Tahiri?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I think you may know better than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You claim -- you're claiming here -- that is to say, you're testifying here about everything that you heard about but didn't see, so that's why I'm asking you. Who killed Tahir Tahiri, who you say was killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's answered that he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You also said that the police killed Ukshin Ukshini because he had lighted a candle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They hit Ukshin Ukshini's house before the paramilitaries arrived in the village, so this happened two or three days after the NATO airstrikes began, by army soldiers who were deployed at the agriculture cooperatives. They fired at his house when they saw a candle lit. They saw the house of an Albanian who was in -- looked better than the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you consider that they shot because somebody had lighted a candle?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying what happened, and that the firing was -- took place in this case because of a candle, of a lit candle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you say, and when they heard your testimony, I was given information that it was from the roof of that house that Ukshin Ukshini had shot at the army, and it is correct that it took place two or three days after the NATO aggression, and it is true that it took place during the NATO attack, and it is true that he shot at the army, and it is true that he died shooting at the army. Are you aware of that? Do you have that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's true. It cannot be true what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's probably true that people are shot for lighting candles. You said that he was shot at and then you said that the house was shelled. Now you have to choose: Was the house shelled or was he shot at? Which of the two is it?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you are alleging here, that because of a candle, of a lit candle, one cannot be shot at from a distance? I mean, that was something that could be done by the Serbian army that was deployed there. His murder, his killing, happened on the 30th of March, in the morning. At 9.30 was the moment when he, Ukshin Ukshini, and his wife were killed, and they were killed by the Serbian forces, who struck terror also among the other citizens and other families who happened to live nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, you said yesterday that his house was shelled. What I'm asking you is: Did they shell his house or did they shoot at Ukshin Ukshini and his people? You have to choose, because you said both these things. So what was it? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of time, we have -- everything happened over two days. The firing happened before, two days before; the killing took place two days after. That's why this may have been created.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you just explain? What is being suggested is that either Mr. Ukshini was shot or his house was shelled. It may be that you're saying that both happened, but perhaps you could make it clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm going to explain this. I said that when the NATO airstrikes began, that night his house was shelled. Maybe they chose his house because they saw a candle lit, because at that moment, nobody fired. Then his murder was committed two days after, after these events that I said, after the shelling of his house. This happened in the morning, not at night. At 9.30 in the morning of the 30th of March. And I think that this is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see it happen?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard this from other eyewitnesses who were close by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Once again, you don't know how he died, but you heard about it. Very well. You went off to Donja Stubla after that and took refuge in the house of other Albanians and stayed there until the 4th of May; is that right? Which means more than a month. You said that there were 20.000 people who had gathered together and that you then decided to go to Macedonia. How come you speak about 600 people immediately after that? How does 20.000 turn into 600 people?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to explain this. There is a time interval. It is about a month, in fact. If the number of the people that I mentioned, about 20.000 citizens that I have stated, I have explained that they were comprised of Albanian inhabitants of Zheger, Lladove, Nosale, Remnik, Budrike e Eperme, Gjylikar, Mogille, and Kuteseve [phoen] villages. These are all villages where Serbian forces were involved in killing, looting, and raiding, burning the homes of Albanians, which forced them to leave. I explained also that on the 15th of March -- sorry, of April, the village of Gjylikar was stormed as a result of which there were six casualties. Two houses were burned and four-- four of the -- four other victims were buried at Stubell e Ulet, in a meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to repeat your testimony of yesterday. What I'm asking you is how 20.000 people turned into 600 people when you started out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said, in fact, in his evidence earlier that the reason was that villagers from other villages came to find refuge there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. I'm trying to explain this to myself, and I'm asking the witness, therefore, to explain to me how 20.000 persons - and that is his claim, that that was the number of people who were there and decided to go to Macedonia - how did they en route turn into 600 people all at once? Where are the remaining 19.400?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He says they came from other villages and it happened over a period. Now, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is right. During -- they came over a long period of time when their villages were being, as I said, looted and raided, and people were being killed by the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they were coming and going, and you, the 20.000 of you who were there includes all of those who came and went from that place and to the place while you were there. Is that the way I should interpret your explanation?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, at what stage did the group amount to 600?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the time over which that happened was long, and the population of Zheger amounts to about 4.000, and it has big families, and they -- other people came from other villages around. The villages were attacked by the Serb forces, and they came to find shelter on that plateau. The population came there, and they were hungry, and they were in want of everything. The aim of the Serb forces was to create a large crowd of people so that they could exercise a mass deportation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How many actually --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Robinson, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question. Of the 20.000, how many actually went to Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that from the 15th of April onwards, they were going in groups, and they were organised spontaneously. And they left from the 15th of April. We have groups of families who set out to flee the country. Every two to three days such groups were formed, and the group I was part of -- there was another group after the 4th of May where the son of my brother was. They also came across Serb forces as they were going towards the border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We're getting away from the matter now. I understand you to say that you -- they went in different groups to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you set out, when you decided to go to Macedonia, that is to say, this group of yours of 600 persons, that you set out during the night lest you be discovered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And the rest of the groups who set off towards Macedonia, set out towards Macedonia, they tried to exploit the opportunity not to be in the sight of the Serb forces, but some of the groups happened to come across those forces and suffer mistreatment at their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you made an effort to go to Macedonia to seek shelter, to get away from that terrain, unnoticed by the army and police?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course all of us in the group did not like to be sighted and come across Serbian forces, because we were aware of what would happen to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was the general opinion that prevailed in that group of 20.000 persons, to get into Macedonia unnoticed, not to be seen by the army and the police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: His evidence had been about the group which he was with. But was it -- what can be asked is this: Was it the general view amongst the 20.000 or so who left for Macedonia that they should try and get there unnoticed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's true. All the people tried not to be noticed by the Serbian army and paramilitaries because they would suffer at their hands. They knew it. This was a symptom which prevailed among the people who decided -- who were forced to flee. They feared deportation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, gentlemen, that it is not right to intervene in this way, because it could be seen quite clearly from the statement made by this witness that there was no deportation. They were fleeing from the battlefields, from the theatre of war. They were even trying not to be noticed by those who were allegedly deporting them. Therefore, this is a striking example -- contrary, that there is no deportation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will go on with the questions, don't you worry, but I'm just trying to draw your attention to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were saying that you were surrounded by the army and the paramilitaries at a particular site when you were in the field, in a field; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were surrounded. In the case of Rrushtaj, the group I was part of was surrounded by such forces who were at that moment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We've heard that. We've heard that yesterday. We heard that yesterday. You explained that first the men were searched and then they put you all together. All things considered, nothing happened to any one of you, and then you proceeded. And then you were ordered to walk for one kilometre. They told you to sit down. And then you said that the commander - I noted that down - the commander with the military and paramilitary forces came to you personally to talk to you, that he came to talk to you, with the military and paramilitary forces and you on the other side, to ask you why you had called NATO in. Please, what did you answer him?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking for the answer I gave to the commander of the Serb units, it was -- that was a conversation which took place under duress, with guns -- machine-guns, barrels, directed at me, and they standing very next to me, asking explanations why we left our homes and what was the intention behind that, why did we ask NATO to come in. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that yesterday. Tell me, what did you answer him? He asked you why you called NATO in. He actually had a conference with you. He, with his paramilitaries and militaries, and you, among those thousands of people in the field, you were conferring as to why you had asked NATO to come in. So what did you answer him?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer I gave at that moment was that I did not personally call NATO in, although the arrival of NATO was as a result of demand of all the population of Kosova. But I was terrified by the Serb forces and Serb soldiers who were there at that moment, and the paramilitaries, who at every moment were ready to execute me if I said something else. As to why we left our homes, I told them that our houses were burned down. And they asked me who burned those houses. I knew that the houses were burnt by the Serbs, by the Serb paramilitary, and the soldiers together, and other people from the village who had been assigned specific duties. Although I couldn't say this to him, that this was committed by the Serbs, but I told them that the houses were burned, but I don't know from whom. I don't know who burned our houses. Then I heard humiliating comments about my nation and my people, and I was being told that: You want to go to Macedonia and then to Albania and then join the KLA. But I told them that that is not true, because I'm leaving together with my family because my house has been burned. And in similar conditions were the rest of the group I was part of, but I was speaking on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then, after that, as you had said, they let you go on and they told you to go to Presevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just say yes or no, please. I don't want to be deprived of more of my time by Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we were ordered to go in the direction of Presheva, but we didn't know what was waiting for us there, because there were other Serb forces there. And on the way, we deviated from that direction, and I've stated that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We heard that yesterday. We heard that yesterday. As you know, everybody -- perhaps those who are following this do not know this, but Presevo is outside the territory of Kosovo. It is in Serbia. Presevo is not in Macedonia. So you were directed to Presevo, but you managed to sneak away, through certain paths that some people knew, and somehow managed to get to the border; is that right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We walked across some other paths and to the border. We did not go to Presheva; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And over there you passed soldiers. Nobody touched you. You said that yourself. You also said that in your written statement, and you said that during your testimony. Nobody asked you for documents, nobody took away your documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not stripped of our documents, but we were mistreated, and the humiliating comments that we heard from them. Every moment they were saying, "We will kill you." They were all obvious, all too obvious.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to draw your attention, gentlemen, to the fact that the first witnesses said that they heard over the radio and the media that the Serbs would take revenge on them, and since that proved to be a notorious lie, because this was not the case, and every knows that, now witnesses are saying that individuals personally explained to them that they would take revenge on them. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic -- Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to stop you. This is not the time for comments. Have you any more questions, please, for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, the question was clear: You were not touched, you were not asked for documents, your documents were not being taken away; is that correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That was his evidence, that the documents were not removed and he wasn't asked for them. He hasn't said that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of this fact, I would like to draw your attention to it once again, because I think that everybody should note that those who are testifying and who are crossing the Albanian border --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can make the arguments in due course. The witness is here simply to be examined. The Court will have seen that there's a difference between what happened to this witness and what happened to others. It will be a matter for us what conclusion to draw. And at the end of the case you can comment, but at the moment, let's just stick to questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question is why, therefore, those who crossed the Albanian border say that their documents were taken away from them and those who crossed the Macedonian or Montenegrin borders claim that their documents were not taken away? Is it perhaps because the Macedonians and the Montenegrins are not going to lie on their behalf?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a pure matter of comment, Mr. Milosevic. It's not a matter for this witness. He said his documents weren't taken; that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were your documents or the documents of anyone in your group not taken away?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that moment, they did not take documents from us, but other groups said that their documents were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We've already heard about this pattern. It's getting to be boring and it's hearsay anyway. In your written statement and later on, you said something to that effect while you were being questioned here, you said that the army shot at a person called Avni, that they killed him. As a matter of fact, you said that they massacred him. And the truth is quite different. This person was retarded. His father stated that they had left him behind, tied up, because he was mentally retarded. The army found him dead and brought him there, and that's when the authorities got this statement from the father, that this is a young man who was mentally retarded, whom they had tied up themselves so that he would not create problems for them. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have heard about this case when I returned, that Mr. Zenani was killed by Serbian civilians of the Zheger village who were armed - those civilians were armed - and that the killing was carried out on the 6th of July. And that was to intimidate the Albanian population from returning to their homes, because they wanted to make it a fact for the Albanians who were deported not to come back, and that was carried out by the Serb forces, and that is how the population felt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are saying that this was done on the 6th of July?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the 6th of July, but the 6th of June. That was six days before the NATO forces came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to read out your written statement. You said now that this was on the 6th of June. That is to say that you were not in Zegra yet when this happened; is that right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was not in Zheger when it happened. I was in the village of Sllupcane, in Macedonia. But I heard about this from the witnesses, from the eyewitnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. You were not in Zegra. Now I'm going to read out to you what you said in your written statement about that killing. This is what your written statement says, the one that you gave: "A few days before the airstrikes began, a man from the village, Avni - I don't know his last name - was going to his home, which was behind my house, a bit further up on the hill. It was evening. Three or four policemen whom I knew were in the field. They were about 400 metres away from him. One of them was called Jova, but I don't know his last name. Another one was called Dragan, but I don't know his last name either. And I did not know the rest. The two I have named were from Zegra. They were shooting from a distance at Avni, and then they walked up and massacred his body, although I don't know why they did that. After killing him, they mutilated the body and carried it away." And so on and so forth, not to take up any more time by reading this. So you wrote something that was completely to the contrary of what you've said over here. My question is: Did you give statements only to the investigator or did you give statements to some other persons as well except for the investigator who put questions to you here in this regard? Who else did you give statements to?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've only given a statement to the investigators, but here I have forgotten to mention the case about which I heard from Hysen Hyseni, who was together with Avni Zenani. He said that Zenani mustn't go home because he will be threatened by the Serb forces, but he did not heed the advice and he went home to collect some stuff in his house, and there he was shot at by armed people who were at a distance of about 500 metres from the hill of Kushlevica. I said that as regards this actual case, I wasn't there present but I was in Macedonia. But I wanted to say that this was told to me by Hysen Hyseni, and the killing was carried out by the Serb forces in the village of Zheger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're now going to adjourn. It's half past ten. Mr. Milosevic, have you got very much more for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few more questions, a few more questions, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. You will conclude in 20 minutes, please, after the break. We'll adjourn now, 20 minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Microphone. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the name Halit Hyseni? He was from your village. Halit Hyseni?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Halit Huseini?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never heard of this name. Maybe it's not exactly written or pronounced in this way. Maybe Halit Hyseni or something else. The name is not familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know about an event when, on the 29th of March, the army intervened in the yard of Halit Hyseni and that they shot at the army from that yard, and then that four persons were arrested who were armed, and they were taken to the military prison in Pristina. Do you recall that event that took place on the 29th of March in your own village?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These -- it's not true that this event has taken place. I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say you don't know. Is it true that you, in 1988, were a cashier of the KLA in Zegra, that you collected money from the local population and that you were caught with money and lists and were taken into custody and detained in the police station but the police released you afterwards? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a cashier of the financial service of Gjilan municipality for Zheger village, and I collected the money to fund the education, the primary and the secondary education. And regarding the interrogation at the police station, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were taken into custody and detained with the money and lists on you.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had all the documents on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You spoke about the area of Zegra and Donja Stubla, which is where 300 KLA members came after the Americans had arrived, and set fire to and razed all Serb houses to the ground. They set the church on fire and destroyed the cemetery. Do you know about that event, when they destroyed the Serb cemetery?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you say about the KLA soldiers destroying the Serb cemetery, that's not true. Maybe some extremists on their way to the village, when they saw their own homes burned down, in sign of revenge, they may have set fire also to the Serbs' houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Serb houses were razed to the ground, and the church too?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you claim that it wasn't done by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not done by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who did it, then?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, maybe some extremist elements in the village, people in the village, in sign of revenge, when they saw their houses burned to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you consider that the KLA is not a terrorist organisation and is not an extremist organisation, as far as I am able to understand your answer. Am I wrong in thinking that or not?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, the KLA is not a terrorist organisation but an organisation that stood up in defence of the people and fought the Serb terror and atrocities perpetrated against the Albanian population of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If they fought against Serb terror, why, then, did they kill so many Albanians? What do you have to say about that? What is your opinion?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they have killed some Albanians who have been involved and cooperated with the Serb forces, that is, traitors to the nation, they may have done such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So several hundred Albanians were traitors of the nation; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe tens [as interpreted] of Albanians who have cooperated with the Serb Secret Service for the interests of Serbia and Yugoslavia, to the detriment of the interests of the Kosova people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How, then, do you explain the fact that when they killed a doctor, an Albanian who was not in a secret service but just working in the general hospital, or they killed a forester who was an Albanian, or a postman working for the state carrying around letters in the mail, or the forester or a local Albanian who the Albanians themselves elected to keep their village safe? Are they all traitors too?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about what you are saying here. Maybe if you could give me names and last names, I might be in a better position to give my feedback.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I will quote some first and last names, although I have enumerated many names so far, but I have names for you too. Do you happen to know, at the beginning of the bombing, many Albanians went to Gnjilane to stay with their relatives there, and during the bombing, they went to visit their properties that were looked after by the Serbs? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know nothing about that. During the time of the bombing, when the Serb forces were in Zheger village, Albanian inhabitants of Zheger who went to Gjilan, as you say, and visited their homes, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a significant number of Albanians stayed on in the village and that the Serbs helped them, being good neighbours? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only about people who were deported, and that no Albanians remained in Zheger village when it was being torched from the 5th of April and onwards. An old man, who was called Ramiz Seferi, Ramiz Seferi, an old man and his wife who didn't leave the village even though the Serb forces, military, paramilitaries, went to their home to mistreat them, but they told them, "Better kill us here than make us leave our home," because they were about in their 90s, and who, after liberation, he died because of old age. He was willingly waiting for his death at his own home rather than have to flee it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But nothing happened to him. Among those who stayed on was Ramish Fazliu, from whose house, probably to thank the Serbs for looking after him during the war, later, when the American KFOR arrived, shooting was done on some young people: Momcilo Zivkovic - he was 20 years old - and a medical student, Sasa Stanojevic. They were seriously wounded and managed to come to a shop owned by a Serb, Jugoslav Mihajlovic, where they were shot at again from Fazliu's house, who was otherwise a member of the KLA and had worked in Switzerland for a long time. Zivkovic, the owner of the shop, was seriously wounded and another man killed. Do you know about that event?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, I have no information about that. As regards this case, I was -- this happened during the time I was in Macedonia, so I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they were treated afterwards with the Americans' bomb-filled base, and later on in Skopje, but you knew nothing about that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Kasim Isufi stayed on in the village and asked -- he asked the Serbs to transport his family, and the Serbs helped him throughout. Do you know about that other case?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe Kosum. I know no Kasim. I know one by the name of Kosum Isufi. Maybe you are talking about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I said Kasum Jusufi. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Kosum is his name. I know no Kasum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Kosum Jusufi. All right, then. Jusufi. Did you hear about that case?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you talking about? That he was -- he stayed on in the village, a man of 90 years of age?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. First of all, I am looking at the transcript, and it says that I asked about Kasim Isufi. I didn't ask about any Kasim Isufi. I asked about Kasum Isufi. But let me repeat the question anyway. In the village, Kasum Isufi stayed on. He remained there. And he was asked -- he asked the Serbs to transport his sons from Gnjilane and they helped him throughout the war. Do you know about that? I didn't mention a rifle. I didn't mention any weapons at all.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the house of Izet Haziri, they left a person who was not able to move? He was a young man. He was locked up, and that when he cried out for help, the Serbs came and helped him, and, together with the police, they managed to transport him to the Gnjilane hospital, where he remained for treatment. Do you know about that particular case?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about the case you are talking here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about Fatim Isufi, Fatim Isufi who was mentally retarded and left alone in the village?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fitim Isufi was not left alone in the village, because there was also his father there. But when the Serb forces entered his house, breaking down his door, the door of his house, his father was feeding the cattle when he heard the noise and the shouts, and he was scared and he stayed there in the cow shed and was waiting to see what was going to happen. Fitim Isufi woke up from his sleep - he was a mentally retarded person - and at that moment he was shot by the Serbian forces. This was testified to by his father Sukri Isufi [phoen]. That is, his father didn't dare leave the cow shed and see what was happening to his son, I mean to see his dead body, because he was afraid that he might have been shot himself. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is true that he died. Is it true that he attacked the policemen and the soldiers with an axe from behind the door and they didn't know that he was -- they didn't know that he was mentally retarded and that that was an unfortunate incident and that is the truth of it? That's what happened. And his father, of course, did not want to see that. He was in the barn.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is not that he didn't want to see, but he didn't dare see his dead body because he feared that he, too, would have been killed. Who is that father that doesn't want -- doesn't wish to see the dead body of his son or daughter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the time is practically finished that we've allotted to you, but you can ask two or so more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand that you had set a time limit. I have several very vital questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, ask them quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll skip over some of them, but I am going to ask others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after the 10th of June, 1999, in the territory of the Gnjilane municipality, 87 Serbs were killed, one Albanian, and five members of other ethnic groups? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? Where did that happen? In what village? In Zheger or where? I am not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the Gnjilane municipality, but I'll read out two names from the village of Zegra itself. Nebojsa Zivkovic, for example, from Zegra village - it happened in Zegra - and Momcilo Zivkovic, on the 22nd of June, 1999, also in Zegra. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that because I was in Macedonia during that time. So I know nothing about what happened with these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about the killed Albanian Daut Morina at the Ferizpetrol pump on the 22nd of August, 2000?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about the killing also of -- that took place in November 1999 and then in March 2000, April 2000, Xhaber Rexhepi, Qamil Ramaci [phoen], Haxhi Agushi, Inekmi Agushi [phoen]? Do you know about them, about those killings? All that happened on your own territory.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about these murders. I don't remember these names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that the Albanian population was cheerful when the bombing started, and these are your words. You said that, for you, it meant the end of Serb rule and the Slav peoples. That's what you said. "The end of Serb and Slavic rule."

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even earlier I said that we used to organise demonstrations against the Serb violence which even before the war took place in Drenica. We have always asked for outside help and assistance because, as the population of Kosova, we felt defenseless and discriminated against, tortured in every segment of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you about what you yourself said. "The end of the rule of Slav peoples, Slav nations." Are you a racist?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know myself to be a racist. I may say that the end of the Serbian and the Yugoslavian government in Kosova, because I cannot imagine Kosova without the presence of Serb elements in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you won't be able to imagine it without the presence of Serb elements. You needn't worry about that. But you said, "the end of Slav peoples, Slav nations." What have you got against the Slav nations, the Slav people?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about the sufferings to which my people were subjected in the course of their history. It is a fact of life that our people have always been suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you something quite different. What have you got against the Slav peoples? Because you said, "The end of rule of Slav nations." The Macedonians are a Slav nation, and you're shooting in Macedonia, killing Macedonians. Do you think that Macedonians should be expelled from Macedonia as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has given an answer. It will be for the Trial Chamber to determine what weight to give it. Now, Mr. Milosevic, two more questions and then the time has elapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many citizens died under the bombs and whether they, too, were cheerful if they were Albanians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The latter part is a comment. Do you know how many people died as a result of the bomb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the -- what kind of bombing? If you mean the NATO bombing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: NATO bombing, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If you talk about the NATO bombing against the Serb forces, I have no information about that, about the casualties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic, one last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you believe that the families of those Albanians who were killed in NATO bombing were also cheerful over the fact that they were being bombed by NATO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a comment. The amici, have you any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honours, only a few matters that Mr. Shabani referred to. I would like to clarify them, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Shabani, awhile ago you said, when Slobodan Milosevic was questioning you about the killing of Avni, that you learnt Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about that only upon your return. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. When I returned, I heard from Hysen Hyseni.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain when -- when you were being questioned by investigator on the 13th of June, the 15th of June, and the 16th of June, precisely in your village in Zheger, at that time you described this event as if you had watched it yourself. How do you explain this?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even earlier, but now in the case of investigators, I have told them, I have mentioned the name, but probably they didn't understand it. Maybe in the course of the interpretation, something, I mean, has not been properly interpreted, because even then I mentioned this during the -- during the investigation. Also I said this. But probably it didn't come out properly during the interpretation, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. You said then that you saw the policeman who did that. You even said to one -- that one of them was Jova, that the other one was Dragan, that they were from Zegra, and you explained from what distance they were shooting, and you described it as if you had been watching all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, in fairness, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- if the amici is putting to the witness that he said he saw, I believe -- I think the Court ought to look at the passage in the statement since both have now cross-examined on this point. In fairness to the witness, to suggest that he said he saw was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you read out what he said, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would you like me to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Just read it out so we can hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. I believe this is the same passage that was put to him by the accused, but the words were: "There was about three to four policemen I knew in the field, about 400 metres from him. One was called Jova LNU --" meaning last name unknown -- "the other was Dragan LNU. The others I did not know. The two I have named were from Zheger." Now, I understand how my friend is suggesting that he saw this. However, the witness is simply saying that the names recounted to him were people he knew. That's -- that is -- and I think -- I have copies of the statement here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'd better have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could copies please be provided? Because he did not mention at all that anybody had told him about this. He was talking about the distance, how they walked up to him, what they did. Not at a single moment does he mention that it was somebody else who told him about this. Please have a look yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I accept the fact that it is not clear that this is something he heard and it does read as if he saw it himself, but he's explained that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us where it is, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It is in the fourth paragraph of the English version, which reads, "start page 2." So the beginning of the statement itself, the cover page being page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please explain? If he cannot explain, I'm not insisting on this. I just feel duty-bound to point this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we have the point, Mr. Tapuskovic. We have the passage in front us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Perhaps I would not have even asked about this had Slobodan Milosevic not referred to it awhile ago. So I thought that this required clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I have an English version of the statement. The last sentence of paragraph 4 is this: "I heard this from a local after I returned." That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first day when you spoke here, you said that in the village that you lived in there were about 70 Serb families, and beforehand you said in this witness statement that we've been referring to that there were 98 Serb houses, Serb families. So which one of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correct version about the number of Serb houses would be -- I said it's not a precise number. I said it's an accurate number because there were some families from Zheger village that lived in some houses in the city. So the number is variable. So in fact, we didn't count the families exactly. More or less this is an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. I do have to go back to what I read out a minute ago. I have carefully read what I read awhile ago and also in reference to what Judge Kwon said. It is the morgue that he refers to as being something that he heard about from a local. So I really have to draw your attention to this. Mr. Shabani was talking about this thing that he was not sure about. He was not sure about what happened at the morgue. So it is not related to the event itself. I have to explain this yet again, because I noticed it only now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I agree with that interpretation, but we have the whole passage, and we'll have to determine what weight to give it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
