utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. However, in relation to the houses, he also said at the beginning of his statement something else, that in that part of the village where the Serb houses were predominantly, between and among these houses there were quite a few Albanian houses as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said around these houses there were also Albanian houses. Around Serb houses there were also Albanian houses. This is what I said. The Serbs were not isolated or the Albanian houses were not kind of clearly divided from the Serb houses in living in certain areas. This is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said clearly last time that those Serb houses that were there had Albanian houses among them as well. That's what you said only yesterday.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only said that around the Serb houses there were also Albanian houses. That is, the Serb houses were not separate from the Albanian houses. They were neighbours. They had only the walls of the houses separating -- of the yards separating them, but they lived in close proximity with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, does that mean that Serb houses were totally surrounded by Albanian houses and that between the Serb houses there were no Albanian houses whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not clear. I'm sorry, I'm not clear about the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If there were Albanian houses around the Serb houses, were there any Albanian houses between and among the Serb houses?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some Albanian houses between and around, and also the same can be said of Serb houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were Serb houses among Albanian houses outside that particular neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not clear. I'm sorry. Can you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what is the relevance of this? Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance will be shown through my next questions. I need to hear -- actually, the witness put it this way: He said that Serb houses were in one part of the village and that among them there were Albanian houses. He said that yesterday. He explained it a bit further today, and then he explained that around the Serb houses there were Albanian houses. I asked him whether among these Serb houses there were Albanian houses as well, and he said yes. And now I'm interested whether beyond that circle where the Serb houses were, were there any Serb houses outside that circle in the neighbourhood where there were predominantly Albanian houses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The question I asked you was what is the relevance of this? How is it going to assist us in trying this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge May, then I have to continue with my questions so that this could be understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Can you explain to us why you are asking these questions. What is the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am putting these questions in relation to the pieces of white cloth that he referred to, that he referred to yesterday. I have to ask about this so that I could put further questions about these pieces of white cloth that he referred to yesterday, and he said that these were an expression of fascism and of fascist genocide. That's the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you ask the question about the white cloth, please, and we can move on more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He said that the Serb families marked their homes by putting a piece of white cloth on the door, and he said that this was an expression of fascism, or rather, the fascist feelings among the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, my question is: Is this the reason, or is it possible that the Serbs put up these white cloths on their houses so that they could perhaps show the houses that no gunfire was coming from?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not true. This means that such -- the idea was, behind the white cloth, that such houses should not be attacked or shot at by people who didn't know, were not familiar with the ground and, because of their ignorance, they might also shoot at the Serb houses, that is, their own troops, their own forces. That's why they did that. White cloths put on their doors was done by the Serbs themselves, as I said, for certain purposes that I just explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the white cloth also a sign of surrender?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at it from -- during the war, in wartime, the white sign might be taken as a sign of surrender, but in this case the Serb forces were present all over the village. So the sign marked out the Serb houses from the Albanian houses, so those could not be targeted at by the Serb forces, who should shoot only at the Albanian houses, which didn't have any white cloth. That was the crux of the matter, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That would suffice, as far as I'm concerned. I'm interested in the following, though: Could this also have been a sign that in these houses with the white flags, there were no members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was only a sign that these houses belonged only to the Serb population. That is all. It has got nothing to do with KLA. Otherwise all the houses, with the exception of those houses with the white sign, would be Albanian houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just interested in one more thing related to this question, and then I will go on. On these white cloths, was there any sign? First of all, was there a fascist sign or any sign on these flags?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from fascist methods used that they tried to separate one identity from another, one house from another, with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just concentrate on the question, please. Was there any sign on the cloth or not? If there wasn't, say so, please.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was only a plain white cloth on their doors. That's what I said, such kind of cloths. I mean, this is what I saw, only that. My house was a little bit far away from these houses. I couldn't see from my home, from that distance, if there were any special signs in these white cloths.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, you said yesterday and today that then you arrived at the village of Donja Stubla. There were no Serb forces or policemen there; right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Lower Stubla, when we went there, at some moments there were no troops. When we were there, the Serb forces arrived. The Serb police came only to see -- to monitor the situation, to see what was happening, and for their own interests, which they know themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, could you explain this. In this statement that you gave to the investigators, you said, verbatim, and I'm reading this: "There were no Serb forces there or policemen." That's the first thing you said. And then you said, on the next page: "The Serb forces never came to Stubla."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I think you should read on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police only went to Gornja Stubla, but not to where they were. Further on in the text, it also says: "The army and the police did not come to Stubla at all." This is the fifth paragraph on that page. So he repeated that four times, and the last time he literally said: "The army and the police did not come to Donja Stubla at all." It is one, two, three, four, five, the fifth paragraph. And they were there for all of five weeks, and the army did Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not come there at all. It's the fifth paragraph. Please. He repeated that four times, and he said, quite unequivocally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we put a question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The question in relation to all of this is the following: He said yesterday that this was a concentration camp, this place where they were quite safe and where the army did not come for all that time, five weeks, and they left there of their own free well, on their own, without any kind of escort. He said yesterday that this was a concentration camp. He did not mention that before, at all, so why did he say that? Why did he say that it was a concentration camp if there was no army or police? If he can explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb army and police were around the village, the villages. That is to say, all the Serb forces were keeping the population under observation. They were monitoring the situation there from the surrounding hills of the village of Stublla, and they had the opportunity to act at any moment, but they knew the time when they would act. All the region was surrounded by the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You had never explained it that way before.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you about what you saw and about what you said. Perhaps it is the way you're putting it right now, but you didn't say that before, and you never said that there was a single policeman or a soldier there. That is what you had said then, and that is what you had said, in a way, over these past two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Tapuskovic. What this witness just said was stated in the witness statement again: I noticed that they were just always observing how many people were in Donja Stubla and the surroundings woods. They were military forces in the surroundings of the village, but they never came into the village. He said that in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Judge Kwon, I did allow for the possibility a while ago that they were somewhere around the village, but he talked about a concentration camp, and they were there for five weeks without having seen a single one. They did not see a single one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I just remind you -- I'd like to remind what he said in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That is a question I shall no longer insist upon. It can be a basis for drawing a conclusion in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also said here that you were being shot at, and you saw what you said you saw. And in your statement, which I'm referring to and which is before the Judges, on page 4 - no, 5 - you said: "They were shooting, but we did not know who they were shooting at or whether they had seen us at all."

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were fleeing, on the way, I have stressed that we were being shot at by the Serb forces from a distance. All the population present there heard the sound of gunshots, and I have stated that, and there were wounded people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not denying that. I'm not challenging that. But you said: "They were shooting, but we did not know who they were shooting at or whether they had seen us at all." However, there was shooting there. Nobody is denying that. There was shooting there, but they were not shooting at you, and you do not know who they were shooting at.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That we didn't know who they were, but we were aware that the Serb forces were shooting at the civilian population, and this is the truth, and I spoke about it earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you also said that your group, the group that you were in, had their money taken away from them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is true. As we were going towards Macedonia, someone who was there, he started to ask us to collect money, to collect the money from us, and he was saying that it were designated for certain purposes, certain things, but I don't know what for. That person was related to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to say yet again what you've been saying yesterday. I just wanted to check whether I had heard it right. But you said before: "They did not ask our group for any money, but later on I did hear that they asked other groups for money." So that's what you said earlier on when you were --

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that other groups ahead of us and other groups that followed us, they were searched and looted by the Serb military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I am just asking you about what you know, and you say that you heard later that others had their money taken away from them, but you only heard about that. That's what you've been telling us; right?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I wasn't there with the other groups, but that's what members of those groups stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You encountered the military. You were going along those roads, as you said - nobody escorted you - and then you crossed the border. When did you see the military? When did you come across the army?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw them in the Rrushtaj village, in one part of the Rrushtaj village. That's where the military came in front of us. That was about 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Near the border?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The border was another ten kilometres further away. So there was another distance to reach the border.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat his question? We could not hear it because he was overlapping the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall be quite direct. I don't want to beat about the bush.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said verbatim earlier on - this is the last paragraph of your statement - "Near the place where we crossed the border into Macedonia, in the trenches there were soldiers. Nobody stopped us, and we did not come across anyone as we were crossing the border." And here you've been saying that you were afraid that you would see the army lest you be massacred. So first and foremost, is it true what you said then, that: "There were soldiers in the trenches where you crossed the border into Macedonia, nobody stopped us, and we did not come across anyone as we were crossing the border"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, could you rephrase it shortly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is hard to rephrase something that is contained in his very own statement. I'm asking him whether it is indeed so, the way he put it here in his statement. "Near the place where we crossed into Macedonia --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just put a short part of the statement to him, a sentence or so, and ask him if it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You saw soldiers in the trenches just before you crossed the border?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army was present, but we were not focusing on that because we wanted to cross the border and it was dark and we don't meet them, and I stressed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody stopped you?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our group was not stopped. We were stopped at the Rrushtaj village. But when we crossed the border, we were not stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were not the victims of a massacre when you encountered the army? And that is what you had feared. This is the only remaining question I have for you.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As can be seen, I was not a victim, because I would have been killed and wouldn't be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: One administrative matter, if I might. Could a number be assigned to the statement that -- might that be marked as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. One question in re-examination, if I might be permitted, for clarification. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, under cross-examination, it was suggested to you by the accused about an incident where you were alleged to be the cashier of a financial service for the KLA. You then gave a response that you were a cashier of some education fund and that you admitted that you were taken into custody for questioning by the police. My question to you simply -- that's the issue I want to direct you to. My question is: Was that cashier's service have anything to do with the KLA, as suggested by the accused?

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It had nothing to do with the KLA. It was exclusively for humanitarian purposes, for educational purposes, for paying teachers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: QAMIL SHABANI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was its purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: One final matter, Your Honour. In cross-examination something was put to this witness for which we do not have documents with us, but we do intend to call another witness later on in these proceedings to provide evidence by way of rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Shabani, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the next witness is called, which you will see on the list that's been provided this morning is a witness called Kadriu, in a position that's been changed from a previous designation of order. It was going to be Witness number 15 in that list, Sakir, who was going to be called this morning. The accused has made a number of comments to me about the change in the order because he had prepared for the witness Sakir this morning, and the change in the order means that he is unprepared to deal with the witness Kadriu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It looks as though he's going to give extensive evidence, judging by the summary. There can be no injustice if he gives his evidence in chief now. We don't call upon the accused to cross-examine. The accused can prepare his cross-examination overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, it's often difficult to explain this matter because we've got an earlier finish to the day today, and of course that witness will still be giving evidence and probably all through tomorrow as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Is there anything you want to add, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. Cross-examination is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. Cross-examination really is the point. If the accused can hold back his position. He is yet unaware how long this witness is going to be, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This witness is going to be some time, Mr. Nice, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a substantial witness, and although I'll do everything I can to make it brief, I think it's likely to take not only today but most of tomorrow's session in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you will not be called to cross-examine this witness who is coming today, and it's likely you probably won't start until Friday, although you may have to make a start tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] The gentleman heard my conversation with the representative of the Registry sitting in front of you there, and she told me during the break a moment ago, she informed me that the order of the witnesses had been changed, and I reacted to that when she told me, I hope with -- I rightly -- I did so

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (redacted) Kadriu on your list. As you know full well, gentlemen, of all the means that I have at my disposal -- actually, I don't have a telephone. That is my only means of communication. And I think, therefore, that it is logical for me to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. expect to have a timetable for one week without its being changed, regardless of whether this is something that the opposite party wants or not, whether it suits the opposite side or not, because I'm able to come by relevant information in that way. In a situation -- in this kind of situation where I have nothing at my disposal except a telephone box in the corridor of the prison, any changes in the order of witnesses directly denies me of this minimum element and means of arriving at the truth with respect to the testimonies and statements of your witnesses. I insist upon being provided with a timetable for the order of witnesses at least a week in advance so that I can act accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the accused has a point. He's representing himself and, therefore, it is more complicated for him than in the normal case if the order is changed. Now, no doubt there's good reason for this change. If you would bear it in mind and keep it -- any changes to a minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I come to deal with that as a matter of urgency, may the comments he made about protected witnesses be redacted from the broadcast to the public, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the other point, he's had lists of witnesses, and of course they always are susceptible to change at the last minute, but he's had the lists available to him for months, and the statements to read. We do our best to notify the changes in the immediate forthcoming witnesses whenever we can. Yesterday's fire is the immediate problem of the latest necessary change, but we'll do what we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before the next witness is called -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry. Just on the matter of the accused's facilities, the amici have filed a motion today relating to provision of assistance for him in the conduct of his defence. There was one motion filed, but it's been re-filed in much more clearer terms, I hope, in its argument. Maybe that would be something that the Trial Chamber might deal with fairly expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we've considered the other one. We need to hear what the Registry say about the present arrangements and any comments they may have, and in fact, we filed an order today ordering the Registry to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before this witness comes in, I've had a request from a member of the press, saying that they are having difficulty in filing copy with witness names accurately spelt because frequently they can't pick up the spelling simply from the name read out, and they are concerned both that they should be professional in what they distribute, and they're also concerned that witnesses shouldn't have their names misspelt, and apparently in the past one or two witnesses have had their names misspelt in a way that makes them barely recognisable. It seems to me that that, if I may say so, is a not unreasonable request. The only way of getting round it, if we don't do what I'm going to propose, is that the press have to come to the Prosecution and seek these details and I'm always concerned to keep to a minimum contact between the press and the Prosecution for obvious reasons. Might it be acceptable to the Chamber when a witness is called to have his name simply revealed on the overhead projector, properly spelt, as I've prepared for this witness, so that it can be accurately reflected in newspapers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. In which case, may Mr. Sabit Kadriu come in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall be adjourning at 12.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While he's coming in -- the witness is being brought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic wants to raise something. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to say the following: This change in the order of witnesses is profoundly one of principle. We cannot, and the accused especially in a day when a witness is to be questioned, be informed that that particular witness will have to be questioned on that day. So we all have to do our duties to the best of our abilities and as far as we are able, and faced with a situation of this kind, when not even the amici curiae know what witness is going to be questioned in advance but when the questioning goes ahead, this goes against the basic principles guaranteed by the Rules and Statute itself. So if we are here to enable and facilitate the work of the Trial Chamber, this should at all costs be avoided in future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it's not a matter of principle. The principle is that the trial should be fair, which means that the accused has sufficient time to prepare for his cross-examination. That we will ensure happens. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, if he may be, can I also inform the Chamber he brought a number of original documents with him in both Albanian and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've managed to get most of them -- to have draft translations. There may be one or two items where the draft translation isn't available. I may be seeking some indulgence there, but it will be very limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would the usher just take this sheet of paper for the ELMO. I'll, in the future, have them typed up, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is your name Sabit Kadriu?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, I'm going to ask you a series of questions to which I hope very short yes or no answers will be appropriate so that we can deal with your background swiftly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be convenient if the Chamber has before it the map which shows Vushtrri or Vucitrn. It's coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But indeed, are you now 41 years old, a Kosovo Albanian Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Having --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Having lived most of your life in Brusnik in the municipality of Vucitrn, with your parents and nine siblings?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Has any member of your family been involved with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Kemajl, who studied in Tirana. After he finished his studies, he wasn't able to return. He was involved there in Tirana.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you, in 1990, become a member of the Council for Human Rights in Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you become its president?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, I was its president, the president of the Council of Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And have you more recently worked as assistant to the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as a result of that, did you cease your work for the Council for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your own educational background is that you were at Pristina University between 1979 and 1984?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we look, please, now very briefly at map 10 of Exhibit 4 so we can begin to familiarise ourselves with the relevant geography. Vucitrn in North Kosovo is shown in the centre of the map. Your village --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- of Brusnik is south-west. Just point it out, please, with the pointer. It's not on the screen maybe. Yes, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: That's where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You'll find that you'll be being asked to point to things on the map. You can probably do it from the seated position if it's more comfortable to you. Mr. Kadriu, I want you to deal with this extremely briefly. It's the last paragraph on page 1. Just yes or no. Was there a memorandum believed to have been published by members of the Academy of Arts and Science of two people, Garasanin and Cubrilovic, a long time ago now, in the 1930s?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think unless anyone wants to ask --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was going to leave it on the basis is that although the witness may find it significant, he can answer questions if asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and move straight on, because I then want to come to 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And again briefly, in 1981, was there an encyclopedia of the history of the peoples of Yugoslavia published and was that a document thought by some to be significant in its - just yes or no - in its reflection of Albanian interests?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. In March or April of 1981, were there student protests?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, there were protests and demonstrations, because of the situation that was created --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's an interruption. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a comment to make. These are things for expert witnesses. This witness cannot speak about matters which are within the realm of expert witnesses, and I think we would be going along the wrong road following this route.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said nothing about this. He's merely referred to some demonstrations by way, as I understand it, of background, and no more. He's not giving expert evidence at all. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you involved in those demonstrations yourself?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I was involved because of the dissatisfaction that was created by the Yugoslavia Encyclopedia that was published then. My people -- which was the third from the point of size --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, it's difficult, I know, especially when observations are made about your evidence. For the time being, if we can deal with things by yes/no answers, we'll move on swiftly, and you can always answer further questions. You were involved in student protests. Two other questions, just absolutely in summary: What happened to people who were protesting? What were the consequences for some of them?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In these demonstrations, we did not demand anything other than Kosovo to be a republic, with a similar status to the other republics of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And the protests continued on the 26th of March and 1st and 2nd of April, and they ended up with mistreatment and, in some cases, killings of those who participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And who, what group or organisation, was controlling or trying to suppress, or whatever it was, these protests?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: It was the Yugoslav government who had engaged all the state apparatus in Kosovo, including other assisting forces from Serbia and the rest of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were troops involved?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: It was mainly special units, but on certain cases there were certain failed moves on the part of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you return from --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Reinforced moves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you return from student life to your home village of Brusnik? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: After I finished my studies, I returned to my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have difficulties finding work at that time? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, I had difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you do your military service between 1987 and 1988?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning again to Brusnik, where you eventually gained work as an Albanian teacher in the Vushtrri school in December 1988 --

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- the ethnic composition of that school being how many Albanian and how many Serbian students, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: There were about 2.700 pupils, students, of which about 250 were Serbian, of Serbian nationality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's time for the adjournment. Speaking for myself, I should say that as far as the accused and the amici are concerned, that any cross-examination about events 20 years ago, to which this witness has referred, will be limited. The relevance of these events is extremely limited, as far as this trial is concerned, as far as I can see, and speaking for myself, cross-examination will also be limited. Yes. We'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, with the change in the status of Kosovo's autonomy in 1989, or thereabouts, was there a movement of young Kosovar Albanians that you became aware of?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. There was all-popular movement, movement joined by the minors, the people, the students, towards Pristina, to voice their discontent, which was great, very great.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My question was unhelpfully asked. My fault. Was there also any population movement, one way or the other, or in perhaps two ways, that you became aware of?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. There was a major movement of the population from Pristina to Mitrovica. All the people rose to their feet out of their discontent resulting from the amendment of the constitution of Kosova. The students in their township, the people at large, they were all moving towards Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there -- I've been told that I'm jumping too quickly in at the end of questions, and I will try and slow down. Was there any movement of Serbs in all within Kosovo that you became aware of?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: During that time - in Vushtrri I'm talking about, in Prelluzhe village - because of this discontent, and in order for it to stop, the Serb population of the village had the reason and the Albanian -- and had driven out the Albanian students out of the school. I think that was the first sign of separating the Albanian students from the Serb students.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. And as a matter of fact, where did most of the relocated students from Prelluzhe go?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Albanian students who were driven out of their school had to have their lessons in Stanovci i Poshtem school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prelluzhe can be seen on the same map, slightly to the south and east of the witness's village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Going back to the question of population movements in general, was there any movement into Kosovo of Serbs at any time, or at about this time, of which you were aware?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: During 1987 to 1989, I was a soldier. I was doing my military service. And I remember very well when the accused came to power, there were Serb movements, not only in Prelluzhe, but also in other towns of Kosova. A very extensive movement was under way, during which women were instrumentalised [as interpreted], demanded the resignation of Fadil Hoxha. I think it was 1987, 1989 -- 1988, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally on this, because I don't want to take too long on it: Do you remember any movements in relation to Velikoreke, which is a village the Court can find south and east or east of Brusnik, on the other side of the railway track?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: During this time, but especially after the wars in Croatia and in Bosnia, but even earlier, a village had started to be built, with all the necessary town-planning facilities, in Velikoreke, and in this village, the population which had left Croatia and Bosnia were settled in this village with the purpose of, I think, changing the ethnic structure of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there an incident at a school or schools involving gas, apparently? If so, can you give us a date and then tell us about the incident, but only in a couple of sentences.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, there was. It happened in 1990. I think it was April. I'm not very sure about the date. At that time, our students were poisoned. There were over 250 students - 253, actually - who were poisoned with a poisonous gas which was used in our school and in other schools of Kosova. This was public knowledge. You could find it in all information media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At that time, were Albanian and Serbian students attending school at the same times or was there some segregation in the time at which they attended?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No. At that time, the principal was a Serb. The Serb students had their lessons in the morning, and only in one part of the school. But in the morning. And in the afternoon, parallel with it, there were the Albanian students who had their -- who went to their classes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document referred to, SK1, for the purposes of the summary is a document that has not been translated. It is a document that deals with this. It is available for inspection if anyone wants to see it. I move on to the Council for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've told us about that. Was it formed in 1990? We know about your position. How many members in Vushtrri did it have?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: At the outset, there were 77 members of the local branch of Human Rights Council of Vushtrri. But later, because of fear and reprisals, the number started to reduce.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the purpose and function of the council in Vushtrri?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The purpose and the functions of this council in Vushtrri was to make public -- to report on the violence, reprisals that were being committed after the deprivation of Kosova's autonomy by the Yugoslav government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And to do so, did you conduct inquiries and receive information from others on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I'm not clear about the question. Can I have it repeated, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you receive reports about human rights violations on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, I did, on a regular basis, because our representatives who were spread out in villages and in towns collected information and then they reported them to Pristina, to the central branch of the Human Rights Freedoms Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you able to record and deal with any violations of the human rights of Serbs? If not, why not?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: At that time, there were no cases of violence exerted against Serbs. However, in some cases, we have taken note of those cases and have reported them to the Council on Human Rights and Freedoms. In some cases, however, we were unable to do so because Serb police forces did not let us go near to the site of the crime or the event and find out what happened. So we did it in semi-unlawful way, I would say, or illegal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving on to the end of 1990. At the end of 1990, were Albanian schoolteachers being paid? If not, explain how it came about.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: At the end of 1990, Albanian teachers stopped to be paid. In this case, we demanded to meet the principal, Slobodan Doknic, and wanted to find out why they were not paid. At the beginning, he said that, "You will not be paid because you do not recognise Serbia as your own state." We went again another time, taking with us a senior professor and met with the principal again, and he answered us that this was the order he had been given and he had to obey the orders coming from higher institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Slobodan Doknic later became mayor and we will refer to him later in your evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In 1991, was there any joint education of students or was there segregation?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In September 1991, we went to school as usual, that is, on the 1st of September. But the principal, Slobodan Doknic, had asked one of the guards to close the door, and he told us that, "This is no longer going to be your school." We tried to enter, but they didn't let us. And as of that day, we started our protest to ask for our school. We held a protest on the 1st and the 2nd, and then on the 13th of that September. The protests were so large, so massive that even the parents of the students participated in them, and they asked for the return of the school facility which they themselves have contributed to building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think my mistake. I allowed you to jump over one topic which I'll touch on very lightly. Do you remember anything happening about the teaching and facilities at school in either March 1991 or May of 1991? Deal with it briefly.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: We were forced to have our lessons in houses, which we called houses schools, in order for our students to be able to get education, because living and -- in the middle of Europe, we considered it a tragedy to be deprived of education. But it was a time that the education primary school was suspended. I don't remember the exact date, but it was so for a couple of months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then returning to the September demonstrations, just yes or no to this: Were the police involved in these demonstrations at all, or in controlling them?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: If you mean the 22nd of September demonstration?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, or the one that I think you've mentioned on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Up to -- yes. On the 13th of September, that's true. We organised a large-scale protest with the participation of students and of parents. This protest was wiped out by police through violence. They used violence against both the students and the parents as well as against our -- us as teachers who were -- many of them were mistreated, and I have evidence to prove that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you yourself injured in any way?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. I was beaten up by the police, together with some other colleagues of mine. Because the police interfered so brutally that the students were unable to leave all at once, so we put up a protection fence in front of the students, and they kept beating us on our backs, we teachers who tried to protect the students.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving ahead, you've already told us effectively and in summary about the parallel school system. Was that run openly or covertly?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: We held it openly, but they considered it as if we were holding it in secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened to teachers as a result of the establishment of this parallel school system?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: They resorted to unprecedented violence. I cannot express here what kind of violence they used against teachers and students. We did work very hard for the students to continue to have their lessons, but the police kept interfering very frequently up until 1997. Often teachers were arrested, detained, and then tried. Some of them have even went to prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You yourself, were you arrested? If so, on how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I remember I was arrested over seven times and sentenced to Mitrovica prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For how long and for what alleged offence?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I was sentenced to 20 days. Usually the accusations, the charges, were so absurd that you cannot imagine. We were accused, for example, as if we were holding illegal lessons. This is what the charge read. I used to have all those documents, but unfortunately they got burned during the war. And then we were sent to the Court. Sometimes we were sentenced to prison. Sometimes we had to pay a ransom and then we could leave if we were sentenced to 15 days or under 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a matter for record, for our records, can you tell us the month and year upon which you were imprisoned for 20 days?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It was May. I'm sorry, I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Was there another incident where certificates had been issued to the students in the parallel system which bore the words "Republic of Kosovo" on the letterhead?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: We were obliged to do that. We wrote our own certificates which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we gave to the students to certificate their performance in school. Those certificates -- if the students were caught having these certificates on them, then they were subjected to violence. They might even be detained in police stations. I myself was arrested for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What happened to you when you were arrested in respect of those certificates? And my apologies for cutting off your answer.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I remember I was arrested along with Professor Xhafer Merovci. He taught French. They arrested us in front of our students, who felt very sad seeing us being taken away by the police. When we were in the police, they started to interrogate us. "Look what you are doing. You are issuing certificates on which you write `Republic of Kosova.'" Then they started to offend us and to beat us up. I will never forget that moment. They beat me on -- struck me with a chair on my back. One held me and the other bit me. Even the other professor was mistreated. And on the next day, even it was Saturday, they took us to the court and the court sentenced us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Moving on from your work as a teacher and focusing on your work for the Council of Human Rights, did you suffer any intervention by the police in respect of your work for the Council of Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, even earlier, in Vushtrri at least, we operated almost semi-illegally because we were prosecuted as a result of our activity. In 1997, we -- some of the activists were arrested. I was one of them too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whereabouts were you when you were arrested and what happened to you after your arrest?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: We were in a cafeteria, in the coffee-shop of the city. It was Friday, if I remember correctly. Large police forces surrounded us. We were drinking a tea. It is a traditional drink in our town. They took us with them. They took us to the police. And then there in the police, they started to interrogate and investigate us, and then me and a colleague, who was forced to leave Kosova later and he is to this day in Switzerland, they sent us for three days to the secret service of Yugoslavia where we were interrogated because of our activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And indeed -- indeed, which police had arrested you in the first place?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: We were arrested by the usual police in uniforms. I remember that at the head of that expedition was the Deputy of the Chief of Police Chief, Luisa Simic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the people by whom you were interrogated were which police force?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The people who interrogated us, who took it over from the civilian police, let's say, to the secret police, one of them was called Dusan Janic. He was a chief police, secret police, and he forced us to speak about the work in the context of the Council for Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By that time, had your council made contact with people from other countries who were interested in human rights violations?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. We had frequent contacts because it was in the general interest to exchange information. And in some cases, our villages border other villages of our communes, so we had to exchange information about what was happening in every of these communes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the secret police have any knowledge or appear to have any knowledge of these contacts of yours with people from other countries?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: We were taken to the secret police by Janic, he was the chief of the secret police, he knew some things because he had asked us in 1995 to give him, or he had taken away from us a document at that time, and he had an idea of our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The KLA, so far as you were concerned, when did you first hear about it as a body?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: If I am right, it was 1991, when, for the first time, through some newspapers, I heard about the creation of the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When, as you understood it, was it first an organised body or force?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: At the beginning, I think, it was not an organised body, as such. For the first time, it appeared in November. I don't remember the exact date. In November, it was, of the last years before the war it came out publicly as the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did it in some period before the war start the process of controlling areas?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In fact, the searches of the houses of Albanians started as early as 1991, until the war broke out. There were no Albanian homes that were not searched or ransacked, under the pretext of arms control, and this control was followed by violence, prosecution, arrest, detention in police station sometimes. In my capacity as chairman of this council, I remember that in one day, MUP has asked up to -- interrogated up to 17, 18 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. That doesn't quite answer the question, which was: As a result of all these things, or for whatever reason, did the Kosovo Liberation Army start to control some areas some period of time before the war?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The KLA started, by the end of -- the beginning of 1998, started to expand its activity in Drenica region.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are now going to move to a topic that is not covered by a map presently before you. It's a map that didn't get admitted at the stage when many of the maps were admitted. It's the map of Srbica or Skenderaj municipality. It can either simply take the next exhibit number, or, were you to want it to stay collected with the other maps, then it could become map 11 of Exhibit 4. I'm entirely in the Court's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's more convenient if it goes into the other maps rather than has a separate number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would respectfully agree. So may the witness then have this map. While they're being distributed, I should say, I know that the amici have asked for a map, and I happen to know that there's a rather convenient booklet road map of Kosovo that's published in Kosovo, and I made arrangements to have them brought up, got enough copies of them for everyone to have a version in Court. I will try and put that in hand, because I think it will probably be helpful. It's rather a convenient size and it's not too big and it's got a good index. The Skenderaj map fits on, really, south-west of the Vucitrn map that we've been looking at thus far, just directly south. I'll get the witness to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you, please, Mr. Kadriu, to tell us about an event that happened at Cirez and Likosane. I gather that for the -- I'm sorry to interrupt. I gather that, for the amici, the reference to the map is K8, if that will help. Back to you, Mr. Kadriu. I want you to help us with something that happened at Cirez and Likosane and on the map we've just got before us for Skenderaj or Srbica, can we find Cirez and Likosane on the right-hand side, the eastern part of the map, and pretty well immediately above the legend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which legend?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The legend on the bottom right-hand corner. Immediately above the legend. Go up from that road. You come to Likosane. It's hard to see. And then above that, you have Cirez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Got it.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. You can see Cirez here and Likoshan, two adjoining villages. But the letters are very small. It is difficult to read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And is this south or south-east or south-west of where you live?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The villages lie south-west of my village, and we are divided from them by Bjeshka e Cicavica. But as the crow flies, we are very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think an overall map will prove increasingly valuable, and I'll try and get these road atlases, as they are, up here as soon as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Kadriu, was there an incident at Cirez and Likosane sometime in February 1998? And if yes, can you give us the date?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, there was an incident. If I remember well, it was the end of February. It must have been 28th of February. In the morning of that date - hopefully I am not wrong about the date - we heard fire shots coming from heavy machine-guns, artillery fire, from the direction of the village of Cirez. Someone came - I was sleeping - and told me that from the direction of Cirez and Likoshan, fire shots are being heard. When I went out, they were very distinct. They were heard not only in our village but also in the Vushtrri town, which is a couple of kilometres away from these villages. They were heard. They came mainly from light anti-aircraft artillery, but also other kinds of fire, artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you do, where did you go, who with? Tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Once we heard the shots, since I was a human rights activist, I was eager to know what was happening. With a brother of mine, we went in that direction. Once we arrived in Dubofc village, we met some people who managed to flee. They were mainly family people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the same map, Dubovac is immediately above Cirez but the other side of a roadway, I think -- or no, maybe a river, but a little bit further up.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. So you went to Dubovac with your brother. Who did you then find at that village?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Once we arrived in Dubofc, we met some residents of those villages who had managed to flee. Not only inhabitants from that village, but also from surrounding village. They told us that the Yugoslav troops had surrounded these villages, especially Cirez and Likoshan, but other troops were from the direction of Cirez, and Dukoshan [as interpreted] was -- were moving in the direction. A war had taken place, they told us, but they didn't know what exactly happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause. What troops were said to be involved? What groups and what troops?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: It was clear that military troops were involved. They were in the rear, because we could see the movements of military troops all around. But mainly there were police forces that I think came to the rescue of the local forces from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Police and troops, was that something you ever saw on other occasions in the course of the history you're going to tell us about?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I may tell you that during this action in Cirez and Likoshan, there were also two helicopters which also shot and fired, but I can testify to the participation of the army in other actions, when, in 1998, 22nd of September, the region of Cicavica --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to come to that later, and I just wanted to ask you a general question: If, as you tell us and as you were told or saw yourself, the police and the army were together in this operation, was that the only occasion you were aware of the police and army operating together, or were there other occasions?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In most of the cases of great interventions, these were done in a coordinated way between the army and the police forces, as the case was on the 22nd of September and in Prekaz and other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move from the 28th of February, if it was, were there any reported Serbian deaths coming to you on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that it was somewhere in Drenica, in a village there, that the police forces had begun to search the house of a person whose name I don't know because they are distant villages. When they went there, they used violence, and the owner, in self-defence, shot back at the Serbian forces. But I can't tell you if there were any casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. The following day, the day after your first visit to Dubovac village, did you go back the day after; and if so, where to, what did you see? Remember, try and keep it very concise for the learned Judges.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to go there myself and find out what happened, because the day earlier I was not very clear about what had really happened. But in my home, an activist of the humanitarian fund, a lady, whose seat was in Pristina - but the centre was in Belgrade, the local seat was in Pristina - came to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. It's not your fault, because it's a new experience, I think, to give evidence, Mr. Kadriu. But it's going to save time if you listen to the question. Where did you go and what did you see on that following day? Just tell us.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, we went together there. We visited Cirez and Likoshan villages. We saw there were several casualties from the Sejdiu family. There were four killed, if I'm not mistaken. Two others were killed from the Cirez village. In Likoshan too, there were 12, not only casualties, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. but people who were massacred, and it's from the Ahmeti family. You may remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, as to these two families that suffered loss, and maybe one or two others, did you see all the bodies yourself?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that at the beginning I visited the Sejdiu family, and I paid homage to those students who were killed. And not far from that house, I went to the family of Rukije, and the woman was shot on her head by a machine-gun operated from a tank. She was observing from the first floor of a house, and half of her skull was destroyed. Later on, after the bodies of the Ahmeti family were taken away by the police, we also saw those bodies and we saw that they were massacred, and we buried them in the middle of the Cirez and Likoshan villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many members of the Ahmeti family was it?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Twelve members of the Ahmeti family, I think. It was only the women who had survived. The rest of the Ahmeti family, the males, with the exception of one of the sons who was working abroad, all the rest were executed, were shot. Just one of them survived, one of the males survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of all the people you've now spoken of, was any of them in any form of uniform at the time that you saw their bodies? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No. At that time, I didn't know of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And at that time that you saw them, was there any evidence of any of them being armed, weapons around them or anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: No. The burial, the funeral was quite grand with the attendance of people from all parts of Kosova, but there were also representatives of the NGOs who were there. We took several pictures, and we passed all the accompanying reports to the Pristina headquarters, and some people from other municipalities joined me in producing the pictures and we took all those pictures to the headquarters in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, in the Ahmeti compound, as well as seeing some dead bodies straight away on your visit, did you also visit a scene where there was a large amount of blood and some other human remains?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: When we went together with the member of the humanitarian fund, we saw the scene where the people -- the site where the people were executed. There were some bushes there, and the people were driven out of their homes and at that very site they were shot. We could clear see the blood. And not only us, everybody could see it. On several occasions we saw limbs, we saw jaws, and it was quite clear that the terror had continued all through the night. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, with brevity, by the time of your arrival, had some of the bodies already been removed to the Pristina hospital?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: The bodies, it's true. We didn't find the bodies there because they were taken to the Pristina hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you subsequently see the bodies, and can you explain something of the condition in which you found them or you saw them when you did see them?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: I remember that they reached the place in lorries, and as far as I remember, some of the relatives of the Ahmeti family were interested to take the bodies from the hospital in Pristina, and they were brought there eventually. So we had to act quickly to take pictures of the bodies, and we noticed that most of the bodies were mutilated. They were in a terrible state. Their genital organs were cut off. And you can see this in the pictures which are now with the Council for Human Rights in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, those we don't have here. If anybody wants them, we can seek to obtain them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I move on to an incident a little later on in the same month or thereabouts, perhaps at the same time, concerning the Jasharis? Can you tell us about that, please.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Several days later, in the same way, in the morning, it was the Jashari family living in Prekaz. Their family home was surrounded, and in the same way, in the morning, we heard gunshots directed towards that house. As we learned later, there were heavy machine-guns, explosions. And we realised that somewhere something was going on --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pause.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: -- and that the house was surrounded by the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. Pause, please. Is Prekaz north-east of Skenderaj on the map?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: [No translation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's south-west of where you were.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: This is where Prekaz is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You brought us to the account you had received of the house being surrounded by Serb forces. We can take this comparatively briefly. How many dead people were found there?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Together with some other activists from Vushtrri, we went there a day or two after the incident had happened when the police forces brought the bodies of the people who were executed in the most savage way at a site where building material was being sold, and that was between Skenderaj and Polac villages, and there we saw the bodies on display. And we helped our colleagues from Skenderaj to take the pictures of these bodies. All of them had been executed, women, girls, men. Some of them were also mutilated, massacred. I had some of these, but some of the material was burned together with my house. But the Council for Human Rights and Freedoms in Pristina has those pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we turn to survivors, were there -- are there some members of the Jashari family yet unaccounted for? If so, how many?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to the bodies that were on display, I don't know of the fate of the members of the Sadik Jashari family. Some of the relatives and members of the family of Sadik Jashari went to the police station in Mitrovica because Skenderaj is part of Mitrovica. They asked the police to help, to help them and come closer to the region to find out about the fate of the rest of the Sadik Jashari family. And they went to the scene of the incident. And I'm talking always on the basis of what an eyewitness told me, but the eyewitness was not allowed to go to the very scene of the incident to see for himself what had happened. And to this day, we don't know what has happened to some of the members of the Sadik Jashari family.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many members then unaccounted for, and can you also tell us how many bodies altogether were found at the scene by you as a result of this massacre?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In Prekaz, there are open graves for some, because people hope that one day they will be returned to be buried there. But it seems like there were some -- some about 60 bodies on display at the site I mentioned where building material was being sold. I can't know -- I can't remember exactly what the figure was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. As a result of these events or perhaps for some other reason, did people move from the Drenica area?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. There was mass movement of the people from the Drenica area. Most of them were coming towards Vushtrri because it was still a safer place. And the road is -- the road passes by the villages where my village is, and we saw a considerable number of people who settled in the Vushtrri municipality, and there we registered the population who was displaced by this action taken against the village of Prekaz and the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was a register created for refugees and are you in a position to produce that as an exhibit? A copy of it, I think.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: At that time, the Red Cross headquarters was interested about the numbers because we could not do everything ourselves. So a list was compiled by that association, and they were telling us about the numbers of the people who had settled there, but that was a very small list because not everybody was listed. And that is a document which shows just the beginning of the displacement of the people from their own villages, and it was a difficult operation to register every single individual who was leaving their homes due to the repression and the reprisals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document produced to us by the witness has handwriting on the back. I haven't had that draft translated. I don't think it's relevant. But if the -- the draft translation is now coming round. If the original document can be laid shortly on the ELMO so that people can see it on the television screens, then when that's been done, if the -- if the original could then go to the witness and a draft translation could go onto the television -- onto the overhead projector. So if you could hand that document now, please, to the witness and put the draft translation on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is the document that's being displayed, headed as the "Register of the number of Albanian refugees sheltered in the municipality of Vushtrri after the Serb police - military massacre in Drenica," and then by number, according to village, is there a list of the number of refugees? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The Red Cross was involved in registering the displaced people, but it was not possible to register every single individual because the movement of the -- the moving around was difficult because there was an increased number of forces in the area. This is just a sample of the big, large numbers that were displaced. And here we have the name of Dr. Ismet Shaqiri who was the president of this association who was providing me with information. And I'm sorry that this kind of material was burned and has disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But in any event, when we look at the name of the village or city and the number of refugees, are we looking at the village in which the refugees ended up or are we looking at the village from which the refugees came? It's pretty obvious that Vushtrri is the village where they ended up. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: Yes. Vushtrri is the town, and they have also settled in the villages around Vushtrri. They were part of the Vushtrri municipality, starting from the Oshlan village and the rest. That is where they had settled and taken shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: And at the end of the list there is a total number of the people who were evacuated, who had left their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the distance from Drenica to Vushtrri where refuge was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Prekaz, the village of Prekaz, to Vushtrri, it's about 16, 17 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Drenica -- so we can follow it, Drenica is a region, is it, or an area? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's how we know the region. It's region of Drenica. That's how we know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why were they able to take refuge in Vushtrri?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were people with children, there were women, there were people who were sick, ill. They had left their homes, and that is the reason why we offered shelter to them and all we had. And that was normal to do with people who had -- who were forced to leave their houses because of the shelling from the artillery and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There was no attack on Vushtrri?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, there was no attacks against Vushtrri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we move on a little, we know that your village was close to Vushtrri. We know where it is. In the spring of 1998, did you become aware of any military presence in the area of your village?

utterances.speaker: SABIT KADRIU
utterances.text: In 1998, I remember about -- there was -- I'm not sure about the exact date, but Serb military troops came and set up camp in our village. It's in a forested area. They set up camp there, and they started to deploy from the barracks of Vushtrri to our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before I move on, can I ask that the previous document be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
